nodes.name: Finite metric space M
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{M} = (V, \delta)$ be a finite metric space.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Requests, location and arrival time
nodes.statement: Consider a set $R$ of \emph{requests}, where each request $\rho \in R$ is characterized by its \emph{location} $\ell(\rho) \in V$ \NotationLabel{model:location} (also referred to as the point that \emph{hosts} $\rho$) and \emph{arrival time} $\mathit{t}(\rho) \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A request set $R$; each request has a location $\ell(\rho)\in V$ and an arrival time $t(\rho)\ge 0$.

nodes.name: Even number of requests
nodes.statement: Assume for the time being that $|R|$ is even.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Unique arrival times
nodes.statement: Notice that $R$ can have multiple requests with the same location (in particular, $|R|$ is unbounded with respect to $|V|$); for simplicity, we assume that each request has a unique arrival time.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Min-cost perfect matching with delays (MPMD)
nodes.statement: The input to an online algorithm for the \emph{min-cost perfect matching with delays (MPMD)} problem is a finite metric space $\mathcal{M}$, provided to the algorithm before the execution commences, and a request set $R$ over $\mathcal{M}$ such that each request $\rho \in R$ is presented to the algorithm in an online fashion at its arrival time $\mathit{t}(\rho)$. The goal of the algorithm is to construct a (perfect) \emph{matching} of the request set --- namely, a partition of $R$ into $|R| / 2$ unordered request pairs --- in an online fashion with no preemption.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Online MPMD: requests arrive over time at points of a known finite metric space and must be matched into pairs online, without preemption.

nodes.name: Time cost and space cost of a request
nodes.statement: More formally, the requests $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ can be matched at any time $t \geq \max \{ \mathit{t}(\rho_{1}), \mathit{t}(\rho_{2}) \}$; if algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ matches requests $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ at time $t$, then it incurs a \emph{time cost} of $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\rho_{i}) = t - \mathit{t}(\rho_{i})$ \NotationLabel{model:time-cost-request} and a \emph{space cost} of $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\rho_{i}) = \delta(\ell(\rho_{1}), \ell(\rho_{2})) / 2$ \NotationLabel{model:space-cost-request} for serving $\rho_{i}$, $i \in \{ 1, 2 \}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Matching $\rho_1,\rho_2$ at time $t$ costs each request its waiting time $t-t(\rho_i)$ (time cost) and half their distance (space cost).

nodes.name: Space and time cost of a request set
nodes.statement: The \emph{space cost} and \emph{time cost} of $\mathcal{A}$ for the whole request set are $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{M}) = \sum_{\rho \in R} \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\rho)$ \NotationLabel{model:space-cost-instance} and $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{M}) = \sum_{\rho \in R} \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\rho)$, \NotationLabel{model:time-cost-instance} respectively.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Total cost (MPMD objective)
nodes.statement: The objective is to minimize $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{M}) = \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{M}) + \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{M})$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Competitive ratio (alpha-competitive online MPMD algorithm)
nodes.statement: Online MPMD algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ is said to be \emph{$\alpha$-competitive} if for every finite metric space $\mathcal{M}$, there exists some $\beta = \beta(\mathcal{M})$ such that for every (even size) request set $R$ over $\mathcal{M}$, it is guaranteed that $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{cost}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{M})] \leq \alpha \cdot \mathrm{cost}_{\adv{\mathcal{A}}}(R, \mathcal{M}) + \beta$, where the expectation is taken over the coin tosses of the algorithm (if any) and $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ is an optimal offline algorithm.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{A}$ is $\alpha$-competitive if its expected cost is at most $\alpha$ times the optimal offline cost plus an additive $\beta(\mathcal{M})$.

nodes.name: Oblivious adversary
nodes.statement: It is assumed that $\mathcal{M}$ and $R$ are generated by an \emph{oblivious adversary} that knows $\mathcal{A}$, but not the realization of its coin tosses.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Competitive ratio of the stilt-walker algorithm
nodes.statement: The main technical result of this paper is a randomized online MPMD algorithm whose competitive ratio is $O (\log^{2} n + \log \Delta)$, where $n$ is the number of points in the metric space $\mathcal{M}$ and $\Delta$ is its aspect ratio.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
also_stated_at: A randomized online MPMD algorithm is presented whose competitive ratio is $O (\log^{2} n + \log \Delta)$, where $n$ is the number of points in $\mathcal{M}$ and $\Delta$ is its aspect ratio.
assumptions: $n$ is the number of points in the metric space $\mathcal{M}$ and $\Delta$ is its aspect ratio
conclusions: a randomized online MPMD algorithm whose competitive ratio is $O (\log^{2} n + \log \Delta)$
nodes.statement_short: There is a randomized online MPMD algorithm with competitive ratio $O(\log^2 n+\log\Delta)$.

nodes.name: Constant lower bounds for 2-point metric spaces
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to develop constant lower bounds on the competitive ratio of online MPMD algorithms already for the special case of a $2$-point metric space (note that this special case generalizes the ski rental problem).
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
assumptions: the special case of a $2$-point metric space
conclusions: constant lower bounds on the competitive ratio of online MPMD algorithms

nodes.name: Competitive ratio must grow with n
nodes.statement: While a $2$-point metric space admits an $O (1)$-competitive online MPMD algorithm, we conjecture that in the general case, the competitive ratio must grow as a function of $n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: the competitive ratio must grow as a function of $n$

nodes.name: Input and output entities of a minimization problem
nodes.statement: To be more precise, consider a minimization problem $\mathcal{P}$ defined with respect to some underlying combinatorial structure $\mathcal{C}$ with a ground set $\mathcal{E}_{\text{in}}$ of \emph{input entities} and a ground set $\mathcal{E}_{\text{out}}$ of \emph{output entities}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Input and output instances
nodes.statement: The input and output instances of $\mathcal{P}$ are multisets over $\mathcal{E}_{\text{in}}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\text{out}}$, respectively.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Feasible outputs and admissible input instances
nodes.statement: For each input instance $I$, problem $\mathcal{P}$ determines a collection $\mathcal{F}(I)$ of \emph{feasible} output instances; input instance $I$ is said to be \emph{admissible} if $|\mathcal{F}(I)| \neq \emptyset$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Admissibility closed under difference
nodes.statement: We restrict our attention to problems $\mathcal{P}$ satisfying the property that for every two input instances $I \subseteq J$, if $I$ and $J$ are admissible, then so is $J - I$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Delayed service operator
nodes.statement: Minimization problem $\Pi$ can be transformed into an online problem with delayed service $\Pi_{\text{on}}$ by applying to it the \emph{delayed service operator}: Each request in $\Pi_{\text{on}}$ is characterized by its \emph{location} --- an entity in $\mathcal{E}_{\text{in}}$ --- and by its arrival time. The algorithm can serve a collection $R$ of yet unserved requests by buying a feasible (under $\mathcal{F}$) output instance $S$ for their location multiset at any time $t$ after the arrival of all requests in $R$. The payment for this service is the cost of $S$ plus the total waiting times of the requests in $R$ up to time $t$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The delayed service operator turns a minimization problem into an online problem whose requests may be served late, paying output cost plus waiting time.

nodes.name: MPMD and other problems as delayed-service problems
nodes.statement: The online MPMD problem MPMD is obtained by applying this delayed service operator to the metric min-cost perfect matching problem, where $\mathcal{C}$ is a finite metric space, $\mathcal{C}_{\text{in}}$ is its points, and $\mathcal{C}_{\text{out}}$ is the set of unordered point pairs (a point multiset is an admissible input instance if its cardinality is even).\footnote{ In the offline version of the metric min-cost perfect matching problem it suffices to consider only sets (rather than multisets) for the input and output instances. The generalization to multisets is necessary for the transition to the online version of the problem. } This operator can also be applied to the vertex cover problem ($\mathcal{C}$ is a graph, $\mathcal{C}_{\text{in}}$ is the edge set, and $\mathcal{C}_{\text{out}}$ is the vertex set), the dominating set problem ($\mathcal{C}$ is a graph and $\mathcal{C}_{\text{in}}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{\text{out}}$ are the vertex set), and many more combinatorial optimization problems.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: MPMD is the delayed-service version of metric min-cost perfect matching; the operator also applies to vertex cover, dominating set, etc.

nodes.name: Rooted tree with leaf set
nodes.statement: Consider a tree $T$ \emph{rooted} at some vertex $r$ with a \emph{leaf} set $\mathcal{L}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Full binary tree
nodes.statement: A \emph{binary} tree is called \emph{full} if every internal vertex has exactly two children.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
differentia: every internal vertex has exactly two children

nodes.name: Parent p(v)
nodes.statement: The parent of $v$ in $T$ (assuming that $v \neq r$) is denoted by $p(v)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Subtree T(v) and its leaf set L(v)
nodes.statement: We denote the \emph{subtree} of $T$ rooted at $v$ by $T(v)$ \NotationLabel{tree:subtree} and the leaf set of $T(v)$ by $\mathcal{L}(v)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Ancestors anc(v)
nodes.statement: The set of ancestors of $v$ (excluding $v$ itself) is denoted by $\mathit{anc}(v)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Depth and height
nodes.statement: The \emph{depth} of $v$ in $T$ --- i.e., the distance (in hops) from $v$ to $r$ --- is denoted by $\mathrm{depth}(v)$ \NotationLabel{tree:depth} and the \emph{height} of $T$ is denoted by $\mathrm{height}(T) = \max_{x \in \mathcal{L}} \mathrm{depth}(x)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Stilt (head and foot)
nodes.statement: A \emph{stilt} in $T$ is an oriented path connecting some vertex $v \in T$, referred to as the \emph{head} of the stilt, with a leaf in $\mathcal{L}(v)$, referred to as the \emph{foot} of the stilt.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Least common ancestor lca(x,y)
nodes.statement: Given two leaves $x, y \in \mathcal{L}$, their \emph{least common ancestor (LCA)} in $T$ is denoted by $\mathrm{lca}(x, y)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Vertex weight function w
nodes.statement: Let $w : T \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ be a weight function on the vertices of $T$ that satisfies (i) $w(v) = 0$ for every leaf $v \in \mathcal{L}$; and (ii) $w(v) < w(p(v))$ for every vertex $v \in T - \{ r \}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Ultrametric induced by (T, w)
nodes.statement: The pair $(T, w)$ introduces a finite metric (in fact, an ultrametric) space over the leaf set $\mathcal{L}$ with distance function $\delta$ defined by setting $\delta(x, y) = w(\mathrm{lca}(x, y))$ for every $x, y \in \mathcal{L}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Tree metric space
nodes.statement: A metric space that can be realized by such a $(T, w)$ pair is referred to as a \emph{tree metric space}.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
differentia: can be realized by such a $(T, w)$ pair

nodes.name: Hierarchically well separated tree (alpha-HST)
nodes.statement: Consider some real $\alpha > 1$. A \emph{hierarchically well separated tree} with parameter $\alpha$ (cf.\ \cite{Bartal1996}), or \emph{$\alpha$-HST} in short, is a tree metric space $(T, w)$ that, in addition to the aforementioned requirements, satisfies $w(p(v)) \geq \alpha \cdot w(v)$ for every vertex $v \in T - \{ r \}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
differentia: $w(p(v)) \geq \alpha \cdot w(v)$ for every vertex $v \in T - \{ r \}$

nodes.name: alpha-HSBT
nodes.statement: We refer to an $\alpha$-HST realized by a full binary tree $T$ (cf.\ \cite{CoteMP2008}) as an \emph{$\alpha$-HSBT}.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
differentia: realized by a full binary tree $T$

nodes.name: Probabilistic embedding into HSBTs
nodes.statement: Consider some $n$-point metric space $(V, \delta)$ of aspect ratio $\Delta = \frac{\max_{x \neq y \in V} \delta(x, y)}{\min_{x \neq y \in V} \delta(x, y)}$ and let $\mathcal{U}$ be the set of all $(1 + \Omega (1 / \log n))$-HSBTs $(T, w)$ over $V$ with $\mathrm{height}(T) = O (\log \Delta + \log n)$ and with distance functions $\delta_{\mathcal{T}}$ that dominate $\delta$ in the sense that $\delta_{\mathcal{T}}(x, y) \geq \delta(x, y)$ for every $x, y \in V$. There exists a probability distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over $\mathcal{U}$ such that $\mathbb{E}_{(V, \delta_{\mathcal{T}}) \in \mathcal{P}}[\delta_{\mathcal{T}}(x, y)] \leq O (\log n) \cdot \delta(x, y)$ for every $x, y \in V$. Moreover, the probability distribution $\mathcal{P}$ can be sampled efficiently.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
assumptions: Consider some $n$-point metric space $(V, \delta)$ of aspect ratio $\Delta = \frac{\max_{x \neq y \in V} \delta(x, y)}{\min_{x \neq y \in V} \delta(x, y)}$

let $\mathcal{U}$ be the set of all $(1 + \Omega (1 / \log n))$-HSBTs $(T, w)$ over $V$ with $\mathrm{height}(T) = O (\log \Delta + \log n)$ and with distance functions $\delta_{\mathcal{T}}$ that dominate $\delta$
conclusions: There exists a probability distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over $\mathcal{U}$ such that $\mathbb{E}_{(V, \delta_{\mathcal{T}}) \in \mathcal{P}}[\delta_{\mathcal{T}}(x, y)] \leq O (\log n) \cdot \delta(x, y)$ for every $x, y \in V$
the probability distribution $\mathcal{P}$ can be sampled efficiently
nodes.statement_short: Every $n$-point metric embeds into a random dominating $(1+\Omega(1/\log n))$-HSBT of height $O(\log\Delta+\log n)$ with $O(\log n)$ expected distortion.
nodes.label: theorem:HSBT

nodes.name: Matching across / on top of a vertex
nodes.statement: Suppose that the algorithm matches requests $\rho$ and $\rho'$ with $\ell(\rho) = x \in \mathcal{L}$ and $\ell(\rho') = x' \in \mathcal{L}$, $x \neq x'$. Let $v$ be some vertex in the unique path connecting $x$ and $x'$ in $T$. If $v = \mathrm{lca}(x, x')$, then we refer to this matching operation as matching \emph{across} $v$; otherwise, we refer to it as matching \emph{on top of} $v$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Active request
nodes.statement: If the algorithm matches request $\rho \in R$ $\rho$ at time $t'$, then $\rho$ is said to be \emph{active} at all times $\mathit{t}(\rho) \leq t < t'$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Active request sets C_v(t), C(t)
nodes.statement: Given some vertex $v \in T$, we denote the set of active requests in $\mathcal{L}(v)$ at time $t$ by $\mathit{C}_{v}(t)$ \NotationLabel{alg:active} and write $\mathit{C}(t) = \mathit{C}_{r}(t)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Odd vertices D(t)
nodes.statement: Vertex $v$ is said to be \emph{odd} at time $t$ if $|\mathit{C}_{v}(t)| = 1 \pmod{2}$; let $\mathit{D}(t)$ \NotationLabel{alg:odd} be the set of odd vertices at time $t$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Odd vertices form vertex-disjoint stilts
nodes.statement: A key observation is that the forest induced on $T$ by the vertex subset $\mathit{D}(t)$ is a collection --- denoted hereafter by $\mathcal{S}(t)$ --- \NotationLabel{alg:stilts} of vertex disjoint stilts. Moreover, if $v$ is the head of a stilt in $\mathcal{S}(t)$ then either (1) $v = r$ is the root of $T$ (which implies that $|\mathit{C}(t)|$ is odd); or (2) the sibling of $v$ is also the head of a stilt in $\mathcal{S}(t)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
assumptions: the forest induced on $T$ by the vertex subset $\mathit{D}(t)$
conclusions: is a collection --- denoted hereafter by $\mathcal{S}(t)$ --- \NotationLabel{alg:stilts} of vertex disjoint stilts

if $v$ is the head of a stilt in $\mathcal{S}(t)$ then either (1) $v = r$ is the root of $T$ (which implies that $|\mathit{C}(t)|$ is odd); or (2) the sibling of $v$ is also the head of a stilt in $\mathcal{S}(t)$
nodes.statement_short: The odd vertices induce a collection $\mathcal{S}(t)$ of vertex-disjoint stilts whose heads are the root or come in sibling pairs.

nodes.name: Stilt heads H(t)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathit{H}(t) \subseteq \mathit{D}(t)$ \NotationLabel{alg:heads} be the set of heads of stilts in $\mathcal{S}(t)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Effective vertices F(t)
nodes.statement: Internal vertex $v \in T - \mathcal{L}$ is said to be \emph{effective} at time $t$ if its two children are odd (which, in particular, means that $v$ is not odd); let $\mathit{F}(t)$ \NotationLabel{alg:effective} be the set of effective vertices at time $t$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Supporting leaves
nodes.statement: Notice that $v$ is effective if and only if its two children are in $\mathit{H}(t)$ and let $S_{1}, S_{2} \in \mathcal{S}(t)$ be their corresponding stilts. We refer to the feet of $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ as the \emph{supporting leaves} of $v$ at time $t$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Online algorithm A and benchmark A*
nodes.statement: We shall apply the aforementioned matching algorithm definitions to both our online MPMD algorithm, denoted by $\mathcal{A}$, and to the benchmark offline MPMD algorithm, denoted by $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Asterisk notation for the benchmark (D*(t))
nodes.statement: To distinguish between the two, we reserve the aforementioned notation system for the former and add a superscript asterisk for the latter; in particular, the set of vertices odd under $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ at time $t$ is denoted by $\adv{\mathit{D}}(t)$ \NotationLabel{alg:adv-odd} (whereas the set of vertices odd under $\mathcal{A}$ at time $t$ is denoted by $\mathit{D}(t)$).
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Discrete time steps
nodes.statement: Although $\mathcal{A}$ operates in continuous time, it will be convenient to describe it as if it progresses in discrete \emph{time steps}, taking the difference $d t$ between two consecutive time steps to be infinitesimally small so that at most one request arrives in each time step.
nodes.section: 3 An online MPMD algorithm

nodes.name: Each leaf hosts at most one active request
nodes.statement: Assume hereafter that each leaf in $\mathcal{L}$ hosts at most one active request.
nodes.section: 3 An online MPMD algorithm

nodes.name: Supporting leaves x_1^v, x_2^v of an effective vertex
nodes.statement: Consider some effective vertex $v \in \mathit{F}(t)$ and let $x_{1}^{v}, x_{2}^{v}$ be its supporting leaves (the feet of the corresponding stilts in $\mathcal{S}(t)$).
nodes.section: 3 An online MPMD algorithm

nodes.name: Supporting requests
nodes.statement: By definition, $x_{i}^{v}$ hosts an odd number of active requests at time $t$ for $i \in \{ 1, 2 \}$ and since it cannot host more than one active request, it follows that there exists a unique active request $\rho_{i}^{v}$ at time $t$ with $\ell(\rho_{i}^{v}) = x_{i}^{v}$; we refer to $\rho_{1}^{v}$ and $\rho_{2}^{v}$ as the \emph{supporting requests} of $v$.
nodes.section: 3 An online MPMD algorithm

nodes.name: Stilt-walker algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{ The operation of $\mathcal{A}$ at time step $t$. } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \If{$\exists \rho, \rho' \in \mathit{C}(t)$ with $\ell(\rho) = \ell(\rho')$} \Comment{there can be at most one such request pair} \State{match $\rho$ and $\rho'$} \EndIf \ForAll{$v \in \mathit{F}(t)$} \State{$x_{1}^{v}, x_{2}^{v} \leftarrow$ supporting leaves of $v$} \State{$\rho_{i}^{v} \leftarrow$ unique active request with $\ell(\rho_{i}^{v}) = x_{i}^{v}$ for $i = 1, 2$} \State{$z = z(v, t) \leftarrow$ outcome of an independent Bernoulli trial with parameter $d t / w(v)$} \If{$z = 1$} \State{match $\rho_{1}^{v}$ and $\rho_{2}^{v}$} \Comment{matching across $v$} \EndIf \EndFor \end{algorithmic}

nodes.name: Proof of the competitive ratio from Theorems 2.1 and 4.1
nodes.statement: To that end, fix some $n$-point metric space $\mathcal{M} = (V, \delta)$ of aspect ratio $\Delta$ and a request set $R$ over $\mathcal{M}$ and let $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{*}$ be an optimal (offline) algorithm for $R$ (over $\mathcal{M}$). Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the probability distribution promised by Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:HSBT} when applied to $\mathcal{M}$. Denoting the coin tosses of $\mathcal{A}$ by $\chi$ and taking $\mathcal{T}$ to be some HSBT in the support of $\mathcal{P}$, we can employ Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:main} to conclude that \[ \mathbb{E}_{\chi} \left[ \mathrm{cost}_{\mathcal{A}} \left( R, \mathcal{T} \right) \right] \leq O (\log n) \cdot \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{T} \right) + O (\log \Delta + \log n) \cdot \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\mathcal{A}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{T} \right) + \beta(\mathcal{T}) \, , \] where $\mathcal{A}^{*}$ is the projection of $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{*}$ on $\mathcal{T}$ (that is, same requests are matched at the same time, incurring possibly different space costs). Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}, \chi} \left[ \mathrm{cost}_{\mathcal{A}} \left( R, \mathcal{M} \right) \right] \, \leq \, & \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T} \in \mathcal{P}} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{\chi} \left[ \mathrm{cost}_{\mathcal{A}} \left( R, \mathcal{T} \right) \right] \right] \\ \leq \, & \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T} \in \mathcal{P}} \left[ O (\log n) \cdot \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{T} \right) + O (\log \Delta + \log n) \cdot \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\mathcal{A}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{T} \right) + \beta(\mathcal{T}) \right] \\ = \, & O (\log n) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T} \in \mathcal{P}} \left[ \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{T} \right) \right] + O (\log \Delta + \log n) \cdot \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{M} \right) + \beta(\mathcal{M}) \\ \leq \, & O \left( \log^{2} n \right) \cdot \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{M} \right) + O (\log \Delta + \log n) \cdot \mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{M} \right) + \beta(\mathcal{M}) \\ \leq \, & O \left( \log \Delta + \log^{2} n \right) \cdot \mathrm{cost}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{*}} \left( R, \mathcal{M} \right) + \beta(\mathcal{M}) \, , \end{align*} where $\beta(\mathcal{M}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T} \in \mathcal{P}}[\beta(\mathcal{T})]$, the first transition holds since the distance functions in the support of $\mathcal{P}$ dominate $\delta$, the third transition holds since the time costs of $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{*}$ in $\mathcal{M}$ are the same as those of $\mathcal{A}^{*}$ in $\mathcal{T}$, and the fourth transition holds by Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:HSBT}.

nodes.name: Alternating Poisson process (APP)
nodes.statement: A major component of the analysis presented in Sec.{}~\ref{section:analysis-heart} is a stochastic process (more specifically, a point process) that we refer to as an \emph{alternating Poisson process (APP)}. This process is parametrized by its \emph{start time} $t_{0} \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, \emph{length} $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$, \emph{rate} $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$, and a right-continuous \emph{coloring function} $c : [t_{0}, t_{0} + \gamma) \rightarrow \{ 1, 2, \bot \}$ with finitely many discontinuity points.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes
nodes.statement_short: An APP is a point process with start time $t_0$, length $\gamma$, rate $\lambda$ and a coloring $c:[t_0,t_0+\gamma)\to\{1,2,\bot\}$.

nodes.name: APP starts at time 0
nodes.statement: For simplicity, in the remainder of this section, we assume that the APP starts at time $t_{0} = 0$; this assumption can be lifted by translating any time $t \in [0, \gamma]$ to $t + t_{0} \in [t_{0}, t_{0} + \gamma]$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes

nodes.name: 1-volume and 2-volume
nodes.statement: Given some $0 \leq t \leq t' \leq \gamma$, we define the \emph{$1$-volume} and \emph{$2$-volume} of the interval $[t, t')$ as \begin{MathMaybe} V_{1}(t, t') = \int_{t}^{t'} \mathbf{1}(c(x) = 1) \, d x \end{MathMaybe} and \begin{MathMaybe} V_{2}(t, t') = \int_{t}^{t'} \mathbf{1}(c(x) = 2) \, d x \, , \end{MathMaybe} respectively.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes

nodes.name: Alternation times
nodes.statement: The APP is realized by independent and identically $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ distributed random variables $Z_{1}, Z_{2}, \dots$ These determine the $[0, \gamma]$-valued random variables $T_{1}, T_{2}, \dots$, referred to as \emph{alternation times}, defined inductively by fixing $T_{0} = 0$ and setting \[ T_{j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \max \left\{ t \leq \gamma : V_{1}(T_{j - 1}, t) \leq Z_{j} \right\}, & \text{$j$ is odd} \\ \max \left\{ t \leq \gamma : V_{2}(T_{j - 1}, t) \leq Z_{j} \right\}, & \text{$j$ is even} \end{array} \right. \] for $j = 1, 2, \dots$ Put differently, the alternation times divide the process into \emph{iterations} so that iteration $j$ lasts from time $T_{j - 1}$ to time $T_{j}$. In odd (resp., even) iterations, the process \emph{digests} the $1$s (resp., $2$s), ignoring the $\bot$s and the $2$s (resp., $1$s). If the iteration did not end by time $T_{j - 1} < t < \gamma$ and $c(t) = 1$ (resp., $c(t) = 2$), then it ends at time $t + d t$ with probability $\pi = \lambda d t$; the iteration ends at time $\lambda$ if it did not end beforehand (an illustration is provided in Fig.{}~\ref{figure:app}).
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes
nodes.statement_short: Alternation time $T_j$ is the latest time by which the 1-volume (odd $j$) or 2-volume (even $j$) since $T_{j-1}$ is at most the Exp($\lambda$) variable $Z_j$.

nodes.name: Meaningful alternation time
nodes.statement: The definition of the alternation times implies, in particular, that if $T_{j - 1} = \gamma$, then $T_{j} = \gamma$; we say that the $j$th alternation time is \emph{meaningful} if $0 < T_{j} < \gamma$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes

nodes.name: Number of meaningful alternation times N
nodes.statement: Let \begin{MathMaybe} N = \max \{ j \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \mid T_{j} < \gamma \} \end{MathMaybe} be the random variable counting the number of meaningful alternation times.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes

nodes.name: Iteration digestions G_j and total G
nodes.statement: Define the $[0, \gamma]$-valued random variables $G_{1}, G_{2}, \dots$ by setting \[ G_{j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} V_{1}(T_{j - 1}, T_{j}), & \text{$j$ is odd} \\ V_{2}(T_{j - 1}, T_{j}), & \text{$j$ is even} \end{array} \right. \] and let $G = \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty} G_{j}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes

nodes.name: Digestion and total digestion
nodes.statement: We refer to $G_{j}$ as the \emph{digestion} of the $j$th iteration and to $G$ as the \emph{total digestion}.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes

nodes.name: Expected digestion of an iteration
nodes.statement: For every $0 \leq t < \gamma$, we have $\mathbb{E}[G_{j} \mid T_{j - 1} = t] = \frac{1}{\lambda} \left( 1 - e^{-\lambda \cdot V_{i}(t, \gamma)} \right)$, where $i = 1$ if $j$ is odd; and $i = 2$ if $j$ is even.\footnote{ Recall that for every $j > 1$, an odd (resp., even) $j$ implies that $c(t) = c(T_{j - 1})= 2$ (resp., $c(t) = c(T_{j - 1}) = 1$). }
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes
conclusions: $\mathbb{E}[G_{j} \mid T_{j - 1} = t] = \frac{1}{\lambda} \left( 1 - e^{-\lambda \cdot V_{i}(t, \gamma)} \right)$
nodes.statement_short: Conditioned on the iteration's start $t$, its expected digestion is $(1-e^{-\lambda V_i(t,\gamma)})/\lambda$.
nodes.label: lemma:APP-low-bound-last-digestion

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: Assume without loss of generality that $j$ is odd and $i = 1$ (the case that $j$ is even and $i = 2$ is proved following the same line of arguments). The design of the APP implies that conditioned on $T_{j - 1} = t$, the random variable $G_{j}$ satisfies $G_{j} \sim \min \{ \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda), V_{1}(t, \gamma) \}$, that is, it is distributed identically to an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda$, truncated at $V_{1}(t, \gamma)$. Fixing $\vartheta = V_{1}(t, \gamma)$, the assertion follows by observing that \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \min \left\{ \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda), \vartheta \right\} \right] \, = \, & \int_{0}^{\vartheta} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} x \, d x \, + \, \vartheta e^{-\lambda \vartheta} \\ = \, & \left. -e^{-\lambda x} x - \frac{1}{\lambda} e^{-\lambda x} \right|_{0}^{\vartheta} \, + \, \vartheta e^{-\lambda \vartheta} \\ = \, & - \vartheta e^{-\lambda \vartheta} - \frac{1}{\lambda} e^{-\lambda \vartheta} + \frac{1}{\lambda} + \vartheta e^{-\lambda \vartheta} \\ = \, & \frac{1}{\lambda} \left( 1 - e^{-\lambda \vartheta} \right) \, , \end{align*} where the second transition is derived using integration by parts with $u(x) = x$ and $v(x) = -e^{-\lambda x}$.

nodes.statement_short: The digestion is a truncated exponential; compute its mean by integration by parts.

nodes.name: Expected total digestion equals E[N]/lambda
nodes.statement: $\mathbb{E}[G] = \mathbb{E}[N] / \lambda$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Alternating Poisson processes
conclusions: $\mathbb{E}[G] = \mathbb{E}[N] / \lambda$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: Let $I_{j}$, $j = 1, 2, \dots$, be an indicator random variable for the event $T_{j} < \gamma$ and notice that \[ \mathbb{E}[N] \, = \, \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P} \left( N \geq j \right) \, = \, \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty} \mathbb{E} \left[ I_{j} \right] \, . \] Recalling that \[ \mathbb{E}[G] \, = \, \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty} \mathbb{E} \left[ G_{j} \right] \, , \] it suffices to prove that $\mathbb{E}[I_{j}] / \lambda = \mathbb{E}[G_{j}]$ for $j = 1, 2, \dots$ To that end, we show that \[ \mathbb{E} \left[ \mathbb{E} \left[ I_{j} \mid T_{j - 1} \right] \right] / \lambda \, = \, \mathbb{E} \left[ \mathbb{E} \left[ G_{j} \mid T_{j - 1} \right] \right] \, \] which establishes the assertion by the law of total expectation. The random variable $\mathbb{E}[I_{j} \mid T_{j - 1}]$ maps the event $T_{j - 1} = t$ to \[ \mathbb{E}[I_{j} | T_{j - 1} = t] \, = \, \mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda) < V_{i}(t, \gamma)) \, = \, 1 - e^{-\lambda \cdot V_{i}(t, \gamma)} \, , \] where $i = 1$ if $j$ is odd; and $i = 2$ if $j$ is even. The proof is completed by Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:APP-low-bound-last-digestion} as the random variable $\mathbb{E}[G_{j} \mid T_{j - 1}]$ maps the event $T_{j - 1} = t$ to $\mathbb{E}[G_{j} \mid T_{j - 1} = t]$.

nodes.name: Time potentials tau_v and tau*_v
nodes.statement: Consider some internal vertex $v \in T - \mathcal{L}$ with children $u_{1}, u_{2}$ and some $0 \leq t_{0} < t_{1} \leq \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}$. The \emph{time potentials} of $v$, denoted $\tau_{v}$ and $\adv{\tau}_{v}$, capture the contributions of $v$ to $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{T})$ and $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{t}}_{\adv{\mathcal{A}}}(R, \mathcal{T})$, respectively, in a certain time interval. They are defined by setting \[ \tau_{v}([t_{0}, t_{1})) \, = \, \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} \mathbf{1}(v \in \mathit{F}(t)) \, d t \quad \text{and} \quad \adv{\tau}_{v}([t_{0}, t_{1})) \, = \, \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} \mathbf{1}(u_{1} \in \adv{\mathit{D}}(t)) + \mathbf{1}(u_{2} \in \adv{\mathit{D}}(t)) \, d t \, ; \] \NotationLabel{analysis:tau} \NotationLabel{analysis:adv-tau} in other words, a $d t$ amount is deposited into $\tau_{v}$ whenever $v \in \mathit{F}(t)$ and into $\adv{\tau}_{v}$ whenever $u_{i} \in \adv{\mathit{D}}(t)$ for $i \in \{ 1, 2 \}$.

nodes.name: Space potentials sigma_v and sigma*_v
nodes.statement: The \emph{space potentials} of $v$, denoted $\sigma_{v}$ \NotationLabel{analysis:sigma} and $\adv{\sigma}_{v}$, \NotationLabel{analysis:adv-sigma} capture the contributions of $v$ to $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\mathcal{A}}(R, \mathcal{T})$ and $\mathrm{cost}^{\mathit{s}}_{\adv{\mathcal{A}}}(R, \mathcal{T})$, respectively, in a certain time interval. An amount of $w(v)$ is deposited into $\sigma_{v}$ whenever $\mathcal{A}$ matches across $v$; an amount of $w(v)$ is deposited into $\adv{\sigma}_{v}$ whenever $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ matches across or on top of $v$. In other words, given two requests $\rho, \rho'$ with $x = \ell(\rho)$ and $x' = \ell(\rho')$, if $\mathcal{A}$ matches requests $\rho$ and $\rho'$, then we deposit an amount of $w(u)$ into $\sigma_{u}$ for $u = \mathrm{lca}(x, x')$; if $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ matches requests $\rho$ and $\rho'$, then we deposit an amount of $w(u)$ into $\adv{\sigma}_{u}$ for every internal vertex $u$ along the unique path connecting $x$ and $x'$ in $T$. Let $\sigma_{v}([t_{0}, t_{1}))$ and $\adv{\sigma}_{v}([t_{0}, t_{1}))$ be the total amount deposited into $\sigma_{v}$ and $\adv{\sigma}_{v}$, respectively, during the time interval $[t_{0}, t_{1})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: We investigate the dynamics of $(X_{1}(t), X_{2}(t))_{t \in \phi}$ and $(Y_{1}(t), Y_{2}(t))_{t \in \phi}$ that take values in $\{ 0, 1 \}^{2}$ (an illustration is provided in Fig.{}~\ref{figure:phase-app}). Observe that a new request arriving in $\mathcal{L}(u_{i})$, $i \in \{ 1, 2 \}$, flips $X_{i}$ and $Y_{i}$ without affecting $X_{3 - i}$ and $Y_{3 - i}$. While $(Y_{1}, Y_{2})$ is affected only by new request arrivals, the dynamic of $(X_{1}, X_{2})$ is tied to the actions of $\mathcal{A}$ too. Specifically, $\mathcal{A}$ can match across $v$ (recall that $\mathcal{A}$ does not match on top of $v$ in the midst of phase $\phi$) only when $(X_{1}, X_{2}) = (1, 1)$ and if $(X_{1}, X_{2}) = (1, 1)$ throughout the infinitesimally small time interval $[t - d t, t)$, then $\mathcal{A}$ matches across $v$ at time $t$ with probability $d t / w(v)$ (depending solely on the coin tosses of $v$), in which case $(X_{1}, X_{2})$ flips to $(X_{1}(t), X_{2}(t)) = (0, 0)$. Moreover, we know that $(X_{1}(t_{0}), X_{2}(t_{0})) = (0, 0)$. Let $(y_{1}, y_{2}) = (Y_{1}(t_{0}), Y_{2}(t_{0}))$. We color the times in $\phi$ using the coloring function $c : \phi \rightarrow \{ 1, 2, \bot \}$ by setting \[ c(t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & (Y_{1}(t), Y_{2}(t)) = (\neg y_{1}, \neg y_{2}) \\ 2, & (Y_{1}(t), Y_{2}(t)) = (y_{1}, y_{2}) \\ \bot, & \text{o.w.} \end{array} \right. \] The key observation now is that the times at which $\mathcal{A}$ matches across $v$ can be viewed as the meaningful alternation times of an APP $\Pi_{\phi}$ defined over the time interval $\phi$ with coloring function $c(\cdot)$ and rate $1 / w(v)$. (Notice that the role of $(y_{1}, y_{2})$ in the validity of this observation is simply to adjust the dynamic of $(X_{1}, X_{2})$, starting with $(X_{1}(t_{0}), X_{2}(t_{0})) = (0, 0)$, to the APP framework in which the first digested color is defined to be $1$.) Taking $N$ to be the random variable counting the number of meaningful alternation times in $\Pi_{\phi}$ and $G$ to be its total digestion, we conclude that $\sigma(\phi) = w(v) \cdot N$ and $\tau(\phi) = G$. The assertion follows by Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:APP-digestion-equals-number-meaningful}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.8
nodes.statement: We investigate the dynamics of $(X_{1}(t), X_{2}(t))_{t \in \varphi}$ and $(\adv{X}_{1}(t), \adv{X}_{2}(t))_{t \in \varphi}$ that take values in $\{ 0, 1 \}^{2}$ (an illustration is provided in Fig.{}~\ref{figure:subphase-app}). By the definition of a $0$-subphase, at any time $t \in \varphi$, either $(X_{1}(t), X_{2}(t)) = (\adv{X}_{1}(t), \adv{X}_{2}(t))$ or $(X_{1}(t), X_{2}(t)) = (\neg\adv{X}_{1}(t), \neg\adv{X}_{2}(t))$; we refer to the former (resp., latter) as an \emph{agreement} (resp., \emph{disagreement}) state of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$. Observe that a new request arriving in $\mathcal{L}(u_{i})$, $i \in \{ 1, 2 \}$, flips $X_{i}$ and $\adv{X}_{i}$ without affecting $X_{3 - i}$ and $\adv{X}_{3 - i}$. While $(\adv{X}_{1}, \adv{X}_{2})$ is affected only by new request arrivals (recall that $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ does not match across or on top of $v$ in the midst of subphase $\varphi$), the dynamic of $(X_{1}, X_{2})$ is tied to the actions of $\mathcal{A}$ too. Specifically, $\mathcal{A}$ can match across $v$ (recall that $\mathcal{A}$ does not match on top of $v$ in the midst of subphase $\varphi$) only when $(X_{1}, X_{2}) = (1, 1)$ and if $(X_{1}, X_{2}) = (1, 1)$ throughout the infinitesimally small time interval $[t - d t, t)$, then $\mathcal{A}$ matches across $v$ at time $t$ with probability $d t / w(v)$ (depending solely on the coin tosses of $v$), in which case $(X_{1}, X_{2})$ flips to $(X_{1}(t), X_{2}(t)) = (0, 0)$, thus toggling the agreement/disagreement state. Define the functions $c_{\text{agree}} : \varphi \rightarrow \{ 1, 2, \bot \}$ and $c_{\text{disagree}} : \varphi \rightarrow \{ 1, 2, \bot \}$ as follows: \[ c_{\text{agree}}(t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & (\adv{X}_{1}(t), \adv{X}_{2}(t)) = (1, 1) \\ 2, & (\adv{X}_{1}(t), \adv{X}_{2}(t)) = (0, 0) \\ \bot, & \text{o.w.} \end{array} \right. \qquad c_{\text{disagree}}(t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & (\adv{X}_{1}(t), \adv{X}_{2}(t)) = (0, 0) \\ 2, & (\adv{X}_{1}(t), \adv{X}_{2}(t)) = (1, 1) \\ \bot, & \text{o.w.} \end{array} \right. \, . \] We color the times in $\varphi$ using the coloring function $c : \varphi \rightarrow \{ 1, 2, \bot \}$ by setting $c = c_{\text{agree}}$ if the subphase starts in an agreement state; and state; and $c = c_{\text{disagree}}$ if the subphase starts in a disagreement state. otherwise. The key observation now is that the times at which $\mathcal{A}$ matches across $v$ can be viewed as the meaningful alternation times of an APP $\Pi_{\varphi}$ defined over the time interval $\varphi$ with coloring function $c(\cdot)$ and rate $1 / w(v)$. (Notice that the role of the $c_{\text{agree}}$ vs.\ $c_{\text{disagree}}$ distinction in the validity of this observation is simply to adjust the dynamic of $(X_{1}, X_{2})$, starting in an agreement/disagreement state, to the APP framework in which the first digested color is defined to be $1$.) Taking $G$ to be the total digestion of $\Pi_{\varphi}$, we notice that $\tau(\varphi) = G$. Moreover, the construction of the coloring function $c(\cdot)$ ensures that $\adv{\tau}(\varphi) \geq 2 \int_{\varphi} \adv{X}_{1}(t) \cdot \adv{X}_{2}(t) d t \geq 2 \min \{ V_{1}, V_{2} \}$, where $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ are the total $1$- and $2$-volumes of $\Pi_{\varphi}$, respectively. The assertion follows by Lem.{}\ \ref{lemma:APP-digestion-equals-number-meaningful} and \ref{lemma:APP-bound-number-meaningful}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.9
nodes.statement: Let $U^{b}(\phi)$ be the set of $b$-subphases of $\phi$ for $b \in \{ 0, 1 \}$. If $U^{0}(\phi) = \emptyset$ and $U^{1}(\phi) = \{ \varphi \}$, then we can employ Obs.{}~\ref{observation:bound-time-cost-1-subphase} to conclude that $\mathbb{E}_{v}[\tau(\phi)] \leq \adv{\tau}(\varphi) = \adv{\tau}(\phi)$. If $U^{0}(\phi) = \{ \varphi \}$ and $U^{1}(\phi) = \emptyset$, then we can employ Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:bound-time-cost-0-subphase} to conclude that $\mathbb{E}_{v}[\tau(\phi)] \leq w(v) + \adv{\tau}(\varphi) = w(v) + \adv{\tau}(\phi)$. Since all but the last subphases of $\phi$ end when $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ matches across or on top of $v$, it follows by the definition of $\adv{\sigma}$ that $|U^{0}(\phi) \cup U^{1}(\phi)| = 1 + \adv{\sigma}(\phi) / w(v)$. Therefore, if $|U^{0}(\phi) \cup U^{1}(\phi)| > 1$, then we can employ Obs.{}~\ref{observation:bound-time-cost-1-subphase} and Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:bound-time-cost-0-subphase} to conclude that \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{v} \left[ \tau(\phi) \right] \leq & \sum_{\varphi \in U^{0}(\phi)} \left( w(v) + \adv{\tau}(\varphi) \right) + \sum_{\varphi \in U^{1}(\phi)} \adv{\tau}(\varphi) \\ = & \, \adv{\tau}(\phi) + |U^{0}(\phi)| \cdot w(v) \\ \leq & \, \adv{\tau}(\phi) + |U^{0}(\phi) \cup U^{1}(\phi)| \cdot w(v) \\ = & \, \adv{\tau}(\phi) + \left( 1 + \adv{\sigma}(\phi) / w(v) \right) \cdot w(v) \\ = & \, \adv{\tau}(\phi) + w(v) + \adv{\sigma}(\phi) \, \leq \, \adv{\tau}(\phi) + 2 \cdot \adv{\sigma}(\phi) \, , \end{align*} where the last transition holds since $|U^{0}(\phi) \cup U^{1}(\phi)| > 1$ implies that $\adv{\sigma}(\phi) \geq w(v)$. The assertion follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.10
nodes.statement: We investigate the dynamics of $(X(t))_{t \in [0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})}$ and $(Y(t))_{t \in [0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})}$ (an illustration is provided in Fig.{}~\ref{figure:time-line-app}). A new request arriving in $\mathcal{L}(v)$ flips $X$ and $Y$. While $Y$ is affected only by new request arrivals, the dynamic of $X$ is tied to the actions of $\mathcal{A}$ too. Specifically, the design of the stilt-walker algorithm ensures that $\mathcal{A}$ can match on top of $v$ only when $X = 1$ (recall that matching across $v$ does not affect the partition of $[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})$ to phases). Suppose that $X = 1$ throughout the infinitesimally small time interval $I = [t - d t, t)$; let $S$ be the stilt in $\mathcal{S}(t')$ to which $v$ belongs for all $t' \in I$ and let $v' \in \mathit{anc}(v)$ be the head of $S$. Then $\mathcal{A}$ matches across $v'$ and on top of $v$ at time $t$ with probability $\pi(t) = d t / w(v')$ (depending solely on the coin tosses of $v'$), in which case $X$ flips to $X(t) = 0$. Since $v'$ is an ancestor of $v$, we know that $\pi(t) < d t / w(v)$. We color the time line using the coloring function $c : [0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}) \rightarrow \{ 1, 2, \bot \}$ by setting \[ c(t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & Y(t) = 1 \\ 2, & Y(t) = 0 \end{array} \right. \] (note that $\bot$, whose preimage under $c$ is empty, is included in the range of $c$ for the sake of compatibility with the APP framework). The key observation now is that the times at which $\mathcal{A}$ matches on top of $v$ can be viewed as the meaningful alternation times of a rate-varying APP $\Pi_{[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})}$ defined over the time interval $[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})$ with coloring function $c(\cdot)$ and rate function bounded from above by $1 / w(v)$ (recall that a rate-varying APP is a generalization of an APP defined in the end of Sec.{}~\ref{section:alternating-Poisson-process} of the full version). \sloppy Taking $G_{\phi}$ to be the digestion of the iteration in $\Pi_{[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})}$ that starts at time $T^{-} = t$, we notice that $\int_{T^{-}}^{T^{+}} X(s) d s = G_{\phi}$; recalling that the definition of $\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{late}}$ guarantees that $\min \left\{ \int_{t}^{\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}} \mathbf{1}(c(t) = 1) d t, \int_{t}^{\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}} \mathbf{1}(c(t) = 2) d t \right\} > w(v)$ for every $t < \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{late}}$, we obtain property (P1) by applying (the rate-varying version of) Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:APP-low-bound-last-digestion} to $\Pi_{[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})}$. Property (P2) holds simply by applying Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:APP-bound-number-meaningful} to the $[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{late}})$-restriction of $\Pi_{[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})}$. To obtain property (P3), we consider the $[\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{late}}, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})$-restriction of $\Pi_{[0, \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})}$, denote its number of meaningful alternation times by $N$, and observe that $|P_{\mathrm{late}}|$ is stochastically dominated by $N + 1$; the property then follows by Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:APP-bound-number-meaningful} since $\min \left\{ \int_{\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{late}}}^{\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}} \mathbf{1}(c(t) = 1) d t, \int_{\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{late}}}^{\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}} \mathbf{1}(c(t) = 2) d t \right\} \leq w(v)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.11
nodes.statement: Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:partition-time-line-into-phases}(P2) ensures that $|P^{0}_{\mathrm{early}}| \leq K + 1$. Let $\phi_{1}, \dots, \phi_{K + 1}$ be the sequence of early $0$-phases, where, for the sake of the analysis, we introduce a suffix of empty \emph{dummy} phases so that each dummy phase $\phi_{j}$, $|P^{0}_{\mathrm{early}}| + 1 \leq j \leq K + 1$, starts and ends at some arbitrary dummy time $\hat{t} > \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}$, thus ensuring that $\tau(\phi_{j}) = \adv{\tau}(\phi_{j}) = \adv{\sigma}(\phi_{j}) = 0$. Fix some $1 \leq j \leq K + 1$ and let $T^{-}$ and $T^{+}$ be the random variables that capture the starting time and end time of $\phi_{j}$. We argue that \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{v, \mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-} = t \right] \, \leq \, O \left( \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \adv{\tau}(\phi_{j}) + \adv{\sigma}(\phi_{j}) \mid T^{-} = t \right] \right) \end{equation} for any $t$ in the support of $T^{-}$. This clearly holds if $\phi_{j}$ is an empty dummy phase (which means that $t = \hat{t}$), so assume that $t < \mathit{t}_{\mathrm{late}}$. Consider the random variable $\mathbb{E}_{v}[\tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-} = t, T^{+}]$ that maps the event $T^{+} = s$ (defined over the coin tosses in $\mathit{anc}(v)$) to $\mathbb{E}_{v}[\tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-} = t, T^{+} = s]$. By Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:0-and-1-phases}, the latter satisfies $\mathbb{E}_{v}[\tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-} = t, T^{+} = s] \leq \adv{\tau}(t, s) + 2 \adv{\sigma}(t, s) + w(v)$. Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{v} \left[ \tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-} = t, T^{+} \right] \right] \, \leq \, & \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \adv{\tau}(\phi_{j}) + 2 \adv{\sigma}(\phi_{j}) \mid T^{-} = t \right] + w(v) \\ \leq \, & O \left( \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \adv{\tau}(\phi_{j}) + \adv{\sigma}(\phi_{j}) \mid T^{-} = t \right] \right) \, , \end{align*} where the last transition follows from Cor.{}~\ref{corollary:low-bound-early-phase-opt}, thus establishing (\ref{equation:bound-single-phase-conditional}) by the law of total expectation. Consider the random variable $\mathbb{E}_{v, \mathit{anc}(v)}[\tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-}]$ that maps the event $T^{-} = t$ (defined over the coin tosses in $\mathit{anc}(v)$) to $\mathbb{E}_{v, \mathit{anc}(v)}[\tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-} = t]$. Using the bound provided for the latter by (\ref{equation:bound-single-phase-conditional}) and applying the law of total expectation, we conclude that \[ \mathbb{E}_{v, \mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \tau(\phi_{j}) \right] \, = \, \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{v, \mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \tau(\phi_{j}) | T^{-} \right] \right] \, \leq \, O \left( \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \adv{\tau}(\phi_{j}) + \adv{\sigma}(\phi_{j}) \right] \right) \, . \] Therefore, by the linearity of expectation, we derive \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{v, \mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \tau(P^{0}_{\mathrm{early}}) \right] \, = \, & \sum_{j = 1}^{K + 1} \mathbb{E}_{v, \mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \tau(\phi_{j}) \right] \\ \leq \, & \sum_{j = 1}^{K + 1} O \left( \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \adv{\tau}(\phi_{j}) + \adv{\sigma}(\phi_{j}) \right] \right) \, = \, O \left( \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{anc}(v)} \left[ \adv{\tau}(P^{0}_{\mathrm{early}}) + \adv{\sigma}(P^{0}_{\mathrm{early}}) \right] \right) \end{align*} which establishes the assertion.

nodes.name: Lifting the end-of-input signal assumption
nodes.statement: We now turn to lift the end-of-input signal assumption, showing that Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:main} holds also without it. Recall that $\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}} = \max \{ \mathit{t}(\rho) \mid \rho \in R \}$ denotes the arrival time of the last request in $R$ and let $C = \mathit{C}(\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})$ and $F = \mathit{F}(\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}})$ be the set of remaining active requests and the set of effective vertices at time $\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}$, respectively. The analysis presented in Sec.{}~\ref{section:analysis-heart} relies on the assumption that upon receiving the end-of-input signal at time $\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}$, the algorithm immediately clears all the requests in $C$ by matching across every vertex in $F$ which contributes $\mathit{c}_{\mathrm{end}}^{\mathit{s}} = \sum_{v \in F} w(v)$ to the space cost of $\mathcal{A}$ (this contribution to the space cost of $\mathcal{A}$ is taken into account in Sec.{}~\ref{section:analysis-heart}). An examination of the matching policy of the stilt-walker algorithm reveals that in reality, the requests in $C$ are indeed cleared by matching across the vertices in $F$, only that these matching operations are not performed immediately at time $\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}}$, but rather at slightly later (random) times, thus introducing an additional contribution to the time cost of $\mathcal{A}$. Specifically, taking $\rho, \rho' \in C$ to be the supporting requests of some effective vertex $v \in F$, notice that on expectation, $\mathcal{A}$ matches across $v$ at time $\mathit{t}_{\mathrm{end}} + w(v)$ which accounts for an additional contribution of a $2 w(v)$ term to the algorithm's expected time cost. Summing over all vertices in $F$, we conclude that by adding \[ 2 \sum_{v \in F} w(v) \, < \, 2 \sum_{v \in T} w(v) \] to the $\beta$ term in Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:main}, we can lift the end-of-input assumption as promised.

nodes.statement_short: Remaining effective vertices fire after expected $w(v)$ extra time, adding at most $2\sum_v w(v)$ to $\beta$.

nodes.name: MPMD with a fixed penalty for clearing requests (MPMDfp)
nodes.statement: In this section, we consider the online \emph{MPMDfp} problem: a variant of MPMD in which the algorithm is allowed to clear any request $\rho \in R$ at time $t \geq t(\rho)$ without matching it to another request, incurring a fixed penalty $p > 0$ (a parameter of the problem), on top of the time cost $t - t(\rho)$ of $\rho$, that adds to its total cost.
nodes.section: 5 A fixed penalty for clearing requests
also_stated_at: We also consider a variant of the online MPMD problem, referred to as \emph{MPMDfp}, in which the algorithm can clear any unmatched request at a fixed penalty.
nodes.statement_short: MPMDfp: like MPMD, but any request may be cleared unmatched at a fixed penalty $p$ plus its waiting time.

nodes.name: Competitive algorithm for MPMDfp
nodes.statement: There exists a randomized online MPMDfp algorithm for $\mathcal{M}$ whose competitive ratio is $O \left( \log^{2} n + \log \Delta \right)$, where $n$ is the number of points in the underlying metric space and $\Delta$ is its aspect ratio.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement: Consider the underlying $n$-point metric space $\mathcal{M} = (V, \delta)$ and let $d = \min_{x \neq y \in V} \delta(x, y)$ and $D = \max_{x \neq y \in V} \delta(x, y)$ be the minimum and maximum distances between any two distinct points in $\mathcal{M}$, respectively, so that the aspect ratio of $\mathcal{M}$ is $\Delta = D / d$. Assume for the time being that the penalty $p$ satisfies $d / 2 < p < 2 D$. Let $\widehat{\mathcal{M}} = (V \times \{ 1, 2 \}, \widehat{\delta})$ be the metric space defined by setting \[ \widehat{\delta}((x, i_{x}), (y, i_{y})) = \delta(x, y) + p \cdot |i_{x} - i_{y}| \] for every $x, y \in V$ and $i_{x}, i_{y} \in \{ 1, 2 \}$. The assumption that $d / 2 < p < 2 D$ implies that the aspect ratio of $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}$ is proportional to $\Delta$. Let $\widehat{R} = \{ \rho_{1}, \rho_{2} \mid \rho \in R \}$, where $\rho_{i}$, $i \in \{ 1, 2 \}$, is defined by setting $\mathit{t}(\rho_{i}) = \mathit{t}(\rho)$ and $\ell(\rho_{i}) = (\ell(\rho), i)$. We construct an online MPMDfp algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fp}}$ with the desired competitive ratio from the stilt-walker algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ as follows. Algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fp}}$ simulates $\mathcal{A}$ on $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}, \widehat{R}$ and handles the requests in $R$ according to the actions of $\mathcal{A}$ on the requests in $\widehat{R}$. Specifically, for every $\rho \in R$, if $\mathcal{A}$ matches $\rho_{1}$ to some request $\rho'_{1}$, located in $V \times \{ 1 \}$, at time $t$, then $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fp}}$ matches $\rho$ to $\rho'$ at time $t$; if $\mathcal{A}$ matches $\rho_{1}$ to some request $\rho'_{2}$, located in $V \times \{ 2 \}$, at time $t$, then $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fp}}$ clears $\rho$ without matching it (paying the fixed $p$-penalty) at time $t$. The design of $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fp}}$ and the fact that $\widehat{\delta}((x, 1), (y, 2)) \geq p$ for every $x, y \in V$ guarantee that \begin{equation} \mathrm{cost}_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{fp}}}(R, \mathcal{M}) \leq \mathrm{cost}_{\mathcal{A}}(\widehat{R}, \widehat{\mathcal{M}}) \, . \end{equation} Moreover, the construction of $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}$ and $\widehat{R}$ ensures that if $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ is an optimal offline MPMD algorithm and $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{\text{fp}}$ is an optimal offline MPMDfp algorithm, then \begin{equation} \mathrm{cost}_{\adv{\mathcal{A}}}(\widehat{R}, \widehat{\mathcal{M}}) \leq 2 \cdot \mathrm{cost}_{\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{\text{fp}}}(R, \mathcal{M}) \end{equation} since $\adv{\mathcal{A}}$ can project the actions of $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{\text{fp}}$ on each side of $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}$, matching $\rho_{1}$ to $\rho_{2}$ whenever $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{\text{fp}}$ clears $\rho$ without matching it. The assertion follows since the stilt-walker algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ is $O (\log^{2} n + \log \Delta)$-competitive for the MPMD problem. Now, if $p < d / 2$, then an MPMDfp (online or offline) algorithm is always better off clearing the requests by paying the fixed penalty than by matching them. Therefore, in this case, the MPMDfp problem over $\mathcal{M}$ can be decomposed into $n$ independent instances of the MPMDfp over a $1$-point metric space. Each such instance (essentially a repeated version of the ski rental problem) admits an $O (1)$-competitive online algorithm, thus so does the whole problem. It remains to consider the case where $p > 2 D$. In this case, we construct the metric space $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}$ slightly differently: first employ Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:HSBT} to probabilistically embed $\mathcal{M}$ in a $(1 + \Omega (1 / \log n))$-HSBT $(T, w)$; then, take two copies of $T$, call them $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, and connect them so that their roots become the children of a new root $\widehat{r}$, extending the weight function $w$ by setting $w(\widehat{r}) = p$. Notice that the resulting metric space is also a $(1 + \Omega (1 / \log n))$-HSBT whose point set can be renamed $V \times \{ 1, 2 \}$ so that $(x, i)$ is a leaf of $T_{i}$ for every $x \in V$ and $i \in \{ 1, 2 \}$. The rest of the construction of $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fp}}$ is unchanged. Although the aspect ratio of the metric space $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}$ in this case may be large (as large as $p / d$), notice that the height of the underlying $(1 + \Omega (1 / \log n))$-HSBT is still $O (\log \Delta + \log n)$, where $\Delta$ is the aspect ratio of $\mathcal{M}$. This establishes the assertion by recalling that the $\log \Delta$ term in the competitive ratio of the stilt-walker algorithm comes from an upper bound on the height of its HSBT.

nodes.name: Case p < d/2

nodes.name: Deterministic stilt-walker algorithm A_d
nodes.statement: In this section, we consider the deterministic version of the stilt-walker algorithm, denoted $\mathcal{A}_{d}$, obtained by replacing the $(1 / w(v))$-rate exponential timer maintained at each internal vertex $v \in T - \mathcal{L}$ with a deterministic $w(v)$-timer. In other words, the matching policy of $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ is similar to that of $\mathcal{A}$ with one difference: If the last time $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ matched across $v$ was at time $t_{0}$ (take $t_{0} = 0$ if $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ still has not matched across $v$), then the next time it matches across $v$ is the minimum $t_{1}$ that satisfies \[ \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} \mathbf{1}(v \in \mathit{F}(t)) \, d t = w(v) \, . \]

nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{A}_d$ replaces each exponential timer by a deterministic $w(v)$-timer: match across $v$ after $v$ has been effective for $w(v)$ time.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.1
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be some large power of $2$ and let $T$ be an $n$-leaf perfect binary tree (with all leaves at depth $\lg n$). Let $w : T \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ be the weight function defined by setting $w(x) = 0$ for every leaf $x$; and $w(v) = (1 + 1 / \lg n)^{\lg(n) - 1 - i}$ for every internal vertex $v$ of depth $i$. Consider the HSBT $\mathcal{T} = (T, w)$ and notice that the distance between any two distinct points in $\mathcal{T}$ is $\Theta (1)$. We name some of the internal vertices and subtrees of $T$ according to the labels in Fig.{}~\ref{figure:specific-lower-bound}. Let $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{d}$ denote the benchmark offline algorithm and take $\epsilon$ to be a small positive real. For every subtree $T_{j}$, $j = 1, \dots, 6$, fix some arbitrary leaf $x_{j}$ and consider the following scenario $\Gamma$ (refer to Fig.{}~\ref{figure:specific-lower-bound} for an illustration): \begin{DenseItemize} \item $2$ requests arrive at time $0$ at leaves $x_{1}$ and $x_{6}$ (one each). $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{d}$ immediately matches these requests. Following that, the sole effective vertex of $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ is $v_{1}$ with supporting leaves $x_{1}$ and $x_{6}$. \item $4$ requests arrive at time $w(v_{1}) - \epsilon$ at leaves $x_{2}$, $x_{3}$, $x_{4}$, and $x_{5}$ (one each). Following that, the effective vertices of $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ are: \\ $v_{1}$ with supporting leaves $x_{3}$ and $x_{4}$; \\ $v_{3}$ with supporting leaves $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$; and \\ $v_{5}$ with supporting leaves $x_{5}$ and $x_{6}$. \item The timer of $v_{1}$ expires at time $w(v_{1})$ and $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ matches (across $v_{1}$) the active requests hosted at leaves $x_{3}$ and $x_{4}$. \item $4$ requests arrive at time $w(v_{1}) + \epsilon$ at leaves $x_{2}$, $x_{3}$, $x_{4}$, and $x_{5}$ (one each). Both $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ and $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{d}$ immediately match the request pairs hosted at $x_{2}$ and $x_{5}$; $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{d}$ also immediately matches the request pairs hosted at $x_{3}$ and $x_{4}$. Following that, the effective vertices of $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ are: \\ $v_{2}$ with supporting leaves $x_{1}$ and $x_{3}$; and \\ $v_{4}$ with supporting leaves $x_{4}$ and $x_{6}$. \end{DenseItemize} Consider the subscenario $\Gamma'$ induced on $\Gamma$ by the time interval $(0, w(v_{1}) + \epsilon]$. The key observation is that at the beginning of $\Gamma'$, $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ had $2$ active requests located at leaves whose LCA is the the root of $T$ ($v_{1}$), whereas at its end, $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ has $4$ active requests located at leaves whose LCAs are the two depth $1$ vertices ($v_{2}$ and $v_{4}$). On the other hand, $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{d}$ started and ended subscenario $\Gamma'$ with no active requests, paying a total cost of $O (\epsilon)$ during that time period. Subscenarios analogous to $\Gamma'$ are now applied in a recursive manner to the subtrees rooted at the depth $i$ vertices of $T$, for $i = 1, \dots, \lg (n) - 3$. This results in $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ having active requests at exactly $n / 2$ distinct leaves of $T$; to clear all of them, $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ will have to pay $\Omega (n)$ in space cost. On the other hand, the total cost payed by $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{d}$ during all these applications is $O (\epsilon n)$ which can be made arbitrarily small. Adding the $O (1)$ space cost payed by $\adv{\mathcal{A}}_{d}$ at time $0$ for matching the first two requests (across $v_{1}$), we conclude that the competitive ratio of $\mathcal{A}_{d}$ is $\Omega (n)$, as promised.

nodes.name: FRT probabilistic tree embedding
nodes.statement: Consider some $n$-point metric space $(V, \delta)$ and let $\mathcal{U}$ be the set of all $2$-HSTs over $V$ with distance functions $\delta_{\mathcal{T}}$ that dominate $\delta$ in the sense that $\delta_{\mathcal{T}}(x, y) \geq \delta(x, y)$ for every $x, y \in V$. There exists a probability distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over $\mathcal{U}$ such that $\mathbb{E}_{(V, \delta_{\mathcal{T}}) \in \mathcal{P}}[\delta_{\mathcal{T}}(x, y)] \leq O (\log n) \cdot \delta(x, y)$ for every $x, y \in V$. Moreover, the probability distribution $\mathcal{P}$ can be sampled efficiently.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Observe that by the definition of HSTs, the rooted trees realizing the $2$-HSTs promised by Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:FRT} are of height $O (\log \Delta)$, where $\Delta = \frac{\max_{x, y \in V} \delta(x, y)}{\min_{x, y \in V} \delta(x, y)}$ is the aspect ratio of the metric space $(V, \delta)$. These rooted trees have arbitrary degrees, whereas Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:HSBT} requires rooted trees with degrees at most $2$. We resolve this obstacle with the help of the following lemma, proved by Patt-Shamir \cite{PattShamir2015}. \begin{lemma}[\cite{PattShamir2015}] Consider some $n$-leaf rooted tree $T$. There exist a (rooted) full binary tree $T'$ and an injection $f : T \rightarrow T'$ such that \\ (1) $f(v)$ is an ancestor of $f(u)$ in $T'$ if and only if $v$ is an ancestor of $u$ in $T$; \\ (2) $\mathrm{depth}_{T'}(f(v)) \leq \mathrm{depth}_{T'}(f(p^{T}(v))) + O (\log n)$, where $\mathrm{depth}_{T'}(\cdot)$ denotes the depth operator in tree $T'$; and \\ (3) $\mathrm{height}(T') = O (\mathrm{height}(T) + \log n)$. \end{lemma} Consider some $n$-point tree metric space $(T, w)$ in the support of the probability distribution promised by Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:FRT} and let $T'$ and $f : T \rightarrow T'$ be the full binary tree and injection obtained by applying Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:Boaz} to $T$. We construct a weight function $w' : T' \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ on the vertices of $T'$ by first setting $w'(v) = 2 \cdot w(f^{-1}(v))$ for every $v \in f(T)$, and then fixing $w'(v) = w'(p^{T'}(v)) / (1 + \Omega (1 / \log n))$ for every $v \notin f(T)$. Lem.{}~\ref{lemma:Boaz} guarantees that $(T', w')$ is a $(1 + \Omega (1 / \log n))$-HSBT. Taking $\delta$ and $\delta'$ to be the distance functions of $(T, w)$ and $(T', w')$, respectively, we observe that \[ \delta(x, y) \leq \delta'(x, y) \leq 2 \delta(x, y) \] for every two points $x, y$ in the metric space(s), thus establishing Thm.{}~\ref{theorem:HSBT}.
